issues.subcategory: Dummy/randomized data presented as study findings
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly states that the results, and even parts of the method, were written using a randomized Qualtrics-generated dummy dataset and will be updated after real data collection. This makes all inferential results uninterpretable as empirical evidence. Yet the abstract and results describe substantive findings as if they were real. This is a critical validity problem because no scientific conclusion can be drawn from simulated/random data unless explicitly framed as a mock analysis plan rather than findings.
issues.quote: Results were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.

issues.subcategory: Contradictory data-collection status
issues.description: The manuscript simultaneously claims that data collection was completed before analyses and that the method/results use dummy randomized data that will be updated after data collection. These statements cannot both be true. This prevents assessment of preregistration timing, analytic transparency, and whether analyses are confirmatory or illustrative.
issues.quote: All measures and manipulations conducted for this investigation are reported, and data collection was completed before analyses.

issues.subcategory: Self-selection into experimental conditions
issues.description: The procedure states that participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions. This eliminates random assignment and creates severe selection bias, making any causal interpretation of condition differences invalid. Because preferences may correlate with donation tendency, sympathy, numeracy, political ideology, charity attitudes, or prior knowledge, condition effects would be confounded.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: Incorrect claim of within-subject design
issues.description: The design is described as a within-subject design, but the tables show different participant counts across cells and the hypotheses compare independent groups across intervention by identifiability conditions. If participants experienced only one condition, the design is between-subjects; if they experienced all conditions, order/carryover effects and repeated-measures analyses are required. This ambiguity affects the appropriate statistical model and interpretation.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables

issues.subcategory: Between-subjects ANOVA used despite stated within-subject design
issues.description: The analysis uses a 2 x 3 ANOVA with residual df = 994, consistent with a between-subjects design, despite the design being described as within-subject. If the study is truly within-subject, the analysis should model repeated observations and participant-level dependence. If it is between-subjects, the manuscript should not describe it as within-subject. Mis-specified independence assumptions can produce incorrect standard errors and p-values.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on donation.

issues.subcategory: Major deviations from original study undermine close-replication claim
issues.description: The replication changes several theoretically central features of the original studies: real donation of earned money is replaced with hypothetical donation, laboratory/student-center context is replaced with MTurk/online participation, stimuli are updated, Study 1 and Study 3 are merged, and intervention is added to the joint condition. These changes affect affective engagement, perceived endowment, demand characteristics, and donation behavior, so the study is not a close-to-very-close replication in the sense claimed.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: Hypothetical donation does not match real donation behavior
issues.description: The primary dependent variable in the original studies involved actual donation of money participants had received. The replication uses an imaginary donation response. Hypothetical donation intentions often differ from incentivized charitable behavior due to social desirability, lack of opportunity cost, and reduced emotional salience. This weakens construct validity for actual prosocial behavior and limits comparability to the target article.
issues.quote: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: Intervention construct changed by applying explicit intervention to joint condition
issues.description: The manuscript applies the explicit intervention to the joint condition to merge Studies 1 and 3. This conflates the explicit deliberation manipulation from Study 1 with the implicit joint-evaluation/statistics manipulation from Study 3. The joint condition can no longer be interpreted as the original implicit debiasing manipulation because it may also include explicit learning.
issues.quote: The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition to reveal a more comprehensive comparison between the explicit and implicit settings.

issues.subcategory: Causal language unsupported under nonrandom assignment and dummy data
issues.description: The manuscript uses causal wording about effects of identifiability, intervention, and perceived impact, but the stated procedure has participants selecting conditions, and the reported results are based on randomized dummy data. Without random assignment and real observations, causal claims about interventions or identifiability effects are not justified.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.subcategory: Sign error/inconsistent direction in post-hoc interpretation
issues.description: The descriptive means in Table 7 imply that the identifiable condition mean across intervention cells is approximately 2.54 and the statistical condition mean is approximately 2.25, but the text reports the opposite, saying statistical victims received higher donations than identifiable victims with M=2.54 for statistical and M=2.24 for identifiable. The sign of the t statistic and the reported d also appear inconsistent. This undermines interpretation of Hypothesis 1.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.subcategory: Incorrect/inconsistent effect-size reporting for pairwise tests
issues.description: The reported Cohen's d values for pairwise comparisons are implausibly small given the reported means and SDs. For example, if identifiable versus statistical donation differs by about 0.30 on SDs around 1.7, d should be around 0.17, not 0.076. The sign of d is also positive while t is negative in Table 10. This suggests the effect-size computation or labeling is wrong.

issues.subcategory: Confidence intervals for Cohen's d inconsistent with significant tests
issues.description: Several pairwise comparisons are marked significant after Bonferroni correction while their reported 95% confidence intervals for d include zero, which is inconsistent if the CI corresponds to the same contrast and alpha level. This indicates either the confidence intervals are not for the tested effect, are incorrectly computed, or are mislabeled.

issues.subcategory: Incorrect or unclear p-value after Bonferroni correction
issues.description: The table labels the adjusted p-value as pBonferroni, but a t value of -2.40 with df=994 has an unadjusted two-tailed p around .016, and a Bonferroni adjustment for three comparisons gives approximately .049. This is plausible, but the text reports p=.049 without clarifying it is adjusted. Elsewhere the manuscript uses p-values inconsistently, making it difficult to determine whether post-hoc decisions use adjusted or unadjusted values.

issues.subcategory: Contrast test mis-specified using one focal condition versus pooled heterogeneous conditions
issues.description: The planned contrast compares the identifiable/no-intervention condition against the mean of all other five conditions, including joint/no-intervention and joint/intervention. This is not equivalent to the original contrast and combines theoretically distinct cells, potentially masking or creating effects. It also does not directly test the predicted interaction that explicit learning reduces donation to identifiable victims but not statistical victims.
issues.quote: contrast the mean difference of identifiable/no intervention on donation with the combination of 5 conditions  (statistical/no intervention, statistical/intervention, identifiable/intervention, joint/intervention, joint/no intervention)

issues.subcategory: Original-study t statistic sign inconsistent with means
issues.description: For the original-study contrast, the identifiable/no-intervention mean is larger than the other-conditions mean, but the reported t is negative. Unless the subtraction order is reversed, this is a sign inconsistency and should be explained. It contributes to confusion in interpreting directionality.
issues.quote: Identifiable/ no intervention | 2.83 | 2.10 | 117 | -4.06

issues.subcategory: Sample-size table duplicated and malformed
issues.description: Table 4 contains duplicate columns for the replication sample and repeats values, including '1000 | 1000' for sample size. This suggests errors in table construction and raises concern about reporting accuracy.
issues.quote: Sample size | Study 1: 121 Study 3: 159 | 1000 | 1000

issues.subcategory: Recruitment and compensation unspecified
issues.description: The manuscript does not report key participant recruitment details, including exact platform implementation, eligibility criteria, compensation amount, geographic restrictions, approval rate filters, language requirements, or whether participants received the donation endowment. These details are necessary to evaluate sample quality, incentives, and replicability.
issues.quote: Compensation | US$5 | Not specified | Not specified

issues.subcategory: Unspecified geographic origin of replication sample
issues.description: The original sample was U.S. American, whereas the replication sample's geographic origin is reported as not specified. Charitable giving, responses to African famine appeals, and trust in charities may differ across countries and cultures. Without reporting or restricting geography, generalizability and comparability to the original study are limited.
issues.quote: Geographic origin | US American | Not specified | Not specified

issues.subcategory: Implausible age distribution from generated data
issues.description: The reported mean age is 67.8 with SD 30.1 and range 18-120, which is implausible for an MTurk psychology sample and likely reflects the dummy Qualtrics random data. If retained in a real manuscript it would require verification, exclusion rules, and discussion. It also illustrates why dummy data should not be presented as participant characteristics.

issues.subcategory: Exclusions not quantified
issues.description: The manuscript states that participants with prior knowledge and those failing attention checks were excluded but does not report how many were excluded for each reason, whether exclusions were preregistered, whether exclusions occurred before or after randomization, or whether analyses were conducted with and without exclusions. This limits reproducibility and creates potential analytic flexibility.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.subcategory: Missing-data handling not described
issues.description: The manuscript does not explain whether incomplete surveys, skipped donation items, missing covariates, or failed manipulation checks occurred, nor how missing responses were handled. Missing-data decisions can affect cell sizes and inferential results, especially for online surveys.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration

issues.subcategory: Preregistration timing unclear/inconsistent
issues.description: The manuscript claims preregistration and completed data collection, but also says data collection was launched at the start of the study period and results are dummy data to be updated. It is unclear whether the preregistration preceded any real data collection and whether the analysis plan was fixed before observing real outcomes. This weakens confirmatory status.
issues.quote: Data collection for the experiment was launched at the start of the study period.

issues.subcategory: Decision rules for post-hoc tests inconsistent and broad
issues.description: The analysis plan states post-hoc tests will be conducted only if effects are significant, but it lists post-hoc tests for main effects and interactions without specifying exact contrasts, family-wise error families, or which outcomes are primary. This leaves substantial researcher degrees of freedom, especially across many feeling variables and multiple conditions.
issues.quote: Bonferroni -adjusted pairwise comparisons  (Note: We conduct the test  only if the effect of identifiability and intervention are significant)

issues.subcategory: Multiple testing across segregated feelings inadequately controlled
issues.description: The manuscript tests six segregated feeling outcomes for identifiability, intervention, and interaction effects, totaling many inferential tests. Only pairwise post-hoc tests appear Bonferroni-adjusted; there is no correction or multiplicity plan for the family of ANOVAs across feelings. The significant perceived-impact result at p=.045 may not survive correction and should be interpreted cautiously.
issues.quote: Segregated feelings include being upsetting, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation (extension)

issues.subcategory: Aggregated feeling scale not justified psychometrically
issues.description: The study combines diverse items—upset, touched, sympathy, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and possibly perceived impact—into an aggregated feeling measure without reporting item wording, scale anchors, reliability, factor structure, or rationale. Some items are emotions, whereas others are moral judgments or efficacy beliefs. Aggregating them may obscure distinct constructs and reduce validity.
issues.quote: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling

issues.subcategory: Perceived impact conflated with affective feelings
issues.description: Perceived impact of donation is treated as a feeling variable in some sections, but conceptually it is an efficacy belief or cognitive appraisal, not an affective reaction. Combining or analyzing it alongside emotions as a 'segregated feeling' may misrepresent the construct and muddle interpretation of affective mechanisms.
issues.quote: Segregated feelings include being upsetting, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation (extension)

issues.subcategory: Hypothesis for perceived impact contradicts reported abstract conclusion
issues.description: The hypothesis states that identifiable victims should elicit higher perceived impact than statistical victims, but the abstract says results supported lower perceived impact when facing an identifiable victim or identifiable victim with statistics. This contradiction indicates conceptual or reporting confusion about the extension.
issues.quote: It is hypothesized that people generally perceive a stronger impact of donation towards an identified victim than unidentified statistical victims.

issues.subcategory: Results contradict extension hypothesis interpretation
issues.description: The post-hoc result reports higher perceived impact for statistical victims than the joint condition, not higher perceived impact for identifiable victims than statistical victims. This does not support Hypothesis 6 as stated, yet the abstract claims support for a different directional hypothesis. The manuscript should distinguish exploratory unexpected findings from confirmatory support.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=3.12, SD=1.43) had a higher rating of perceived impact of their donation to help the victims than they faced an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics (M=2.85, SD=1.34).

issues.subcategory: Merging two original studies changes manipulation structure
issues.description: Combining Studies 1 and 3 into a single experiment changes the factorial structure and may introduce confounds not present in either original study. The original Study 1 tested explicit intervention in identifiable versus statistical conditions; Study 3 tested a three-condition design without explicit intervention. Combining them into a 2 x 3 design changes context, comparison sets, and possible demand effects.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect

issues.subcategory: Manipulation checks absent or unreported
issues.description: The manuscript does not report whether participants understood the explicit intervention, perceived the victim as identifiable/statistical, noticed or processed the statistics in the joint condition, or engaged in deliberative thinking. Without manipulation checks, null findings cannot be distinguished from failed manipulations.
issues.quote: participants under manipulation were taught about the identifiable victim effect before donating to the victims

issues.subcategory: Stimulus materials insufficiently described in manuscript
issues.description: The manuscript says updated victim information will be retrieved from Save the Children but does not provide the exact text, victim attributes, statistics, images, charity request wording, or whether stimuli were matched for length, vividness, severity, and credibility. Relying on external links is insufficient for review and future replication.
issues.quote: We will present the participants with the most updated victim information retrieved from the website of Save the Children given that those used in the original study was dated two decades ago.

issues.subcategory: Online MTurk setting may increase inattentiveness and demand effects
issues.description: The shift from in-person laboratory/student-center donation to an online survey on MTurk changes participant engagement, perceived realism, attention, and social context. These are not merely contextual details for a donation/affect study and may moderate the identifiable victim effect. The manuscript does not adequately address how online quality was ensured beyond an unspecified attention check.
issues.quote: Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.subcategory: Attention check details missing
issues.description: The manuscript mentions excluding participants who failed an attention check but does not describe the attention-check item, timing, pass criteria, whether multiple attempts were allowed, or whether the check could differentially affect conditions. This impairs reproducibility and assessment of exclusion bias.
issues.quote: those who failed the attention check

issues.subcategory: Ordinal donation outcome analyzed only with ANOVA
issues.description: Donation ranges from $0 to $5, likely a bounded discrete/ordinal variable with non-normal distributions and possible floor/ceiling effects. The original study reportedly used ordered probit in addition to ANOVA, but the replication omits it without justification. ANOVA may be acceptable as a robustness check, but ordinal/bounded models or nonparametric sensitivity analyses should be considered.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression ... This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.subcategory: ANOVA confidence intervals for partial eta squared unclear
issues.description: The manuscript reports 95% CIs for partial eta squared with lower bounds of 0.00 for all effects but does not specify the method used, whether intervals are one-sided/two-sided, or whether they are compatible with the reported F statistics. Effect-size interval estimation for ηp² requires clear methodology for replication.
issues.quote: We conducted the data analysis with JAMOVI for statistical testing and R for calculation of 95%CI given that such function is not available for ANOVA testing in JAMOVI.

issues.subcategory: Power analysis insufficiently reported
issues.description: The manuscript claims the study was powered based on original effects, but it does not report the target effect, alpha, desired power, allocation ratio, primary test, assumed design, or resulting required N in the main text. Given the design changes from 2x2/3-cell to 2x3 and hypothetical donation, the original effect size may not be appropriate for power planning.
issues.quote: The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study. The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary

issues.subcategory: Effect sizes from original interactions reported as Cohen's d without clear derivation
issues.description: The manuscript reports original main and interaction effects as d values, including an interaction effect d = 0.41, but does not explain how d was derived from ANOVA F statistics or whether it represents a standardized mean difference, contrast effect, or interaction contrast. Mislabeling interaction effect sizes as Cohen's d can mislead power analysis and replication evaluation.
issues.quote: The interaction effect was d = 0.41, 95% CI [0.05, 0.77] when explicit learning was adopted to debias the identifiable victim effect.

issues.subcategory: Typographical/malformed hypothesis table obscures hypotheses
issues.description: Hypotheses 5a and 5b are merged into a single table cell with unclear formatting. This makes it difficult to determine the exact predictions and primary tests for affective feelings.
issues.quote: 5a   5b | An identifiable victim elicits more affective feelings than an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics and statistical victims  Learning about the identifiable victim effect elicits less affective feelings towards an identifiable victim and identifiable victims with victim statistics but not towards statistical victims

issues.subcategory: Misclassification of implicit learning/intervention
issues.description: The manuscript describes the joint presentation of identifiable and statistical victim information as 'implicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect.' However, joint evaluation may activate comparison or proportional reasoning but does not necessarily constitute learning about the effect. The term 'learning' implies acquisition of knowledge and should be distinguished from implicit deliberation or comparative evaluation.
issues.quote: participants implicitly learning about the effect would not be presented with such information but with the provision of victim statistics in the identifiable victim condition.

issues.subcategory: Overstatement of identifiable victim effect as unfairness/inefficiency
issues.description: The introduction frames the identifiable victim effect as demonstrating unfairness and inefficient resource allocation, but the experiment only measures small hypothetical donations to specific stimuli. It does not assess fairness judgments, social welfare maximization, actual resource allocation efficiency, or opportunity costs across charities. The conceptual framing overreaches the operational measures.
issues.quote: The inconsistent prosocial motivation not only demonstrates human sense of unfairness in valuing life, but also highlights the lack of efficiency in resource allocation

issues.subcategory: Overclaiming implications despite sample and design limitations
issues.description: The manuscript invokes broad implications for fundraising campaigns and moral responses to genocide, but the proposed sample is MTurk/online with hypothetical $0-$5 donations to Save the Children stimuli. These limitations constrain inference to real-world charitable giving, high-stakes policy, or mass-atrocity response.
issues.quote: the significance of the identifiable victim effect is still crucial to encourage altruistic behaviour towards the needy, especially adopted widely in the fundraising campaign to promote charitable giving.

issues.subcategory: No ethical approval or consent information
issues.description: The manuscript does not report institutional review board/ethics approval, informed consent procedures, deception, debriefing, or handling of charitable-donation framing in a hypothetical online task. These details are important for evaluating ethical conduct and replication.
issues.quote: Full open-science details and disclosures are provided in the supplementary.

issues.subcategory: No blinding or experimenter-control discussion
issues.description: Although online surveys reduce experimenter influence, the manuscript does not describe whether condition assignment, data cleaning, exclusion decisions, or analyses were blinded to condition. Given researcher degrees of freedom in exclusions and analysis, lack of blinding or independent verification can bias results.
issues.quote: Gilad supervised each step in the project, conducted the pre-registrations, and ran data collection.

issues.subcategory: Cell allocation and randomization procedures missing
issues.description: The manuscript provides final cell sizes but does not explain how participants were allocated to the six cells, whether allocation was equal, whether Qualtrics randomizer was used, or whether any blocks/quotas were applied. This is especially problematic because the procedure says participants selected conditions.
issues.quote: Table 7 Descriptive statistics for donation across conditions

issues.subcategory: Cell counts inconsistent with random self-selection claim
issues.description: The six cell counts are relatively balanced and sum to 1000, suggesting random or quota allocation, but the procedure says participants selected preferred conditions. The manuscript needs to resolve whether allocation was randomized, quota-based, or self-selected.

issues.subcategory: No description of prior-knowledge exclusion item
issues.description: Participants with prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, but the manuscript does not give the exact item, response scale, threshold for exclusion, or whether the item was administered before or after the manipulation. Asking after exposure could confound exclusion with treatment.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded

issues.subcategory: Use of 'statistical victim' singular in interpretation
issues.description: The manuscript sometimes refers to 'a statistical victim,' whereas the construct concerns statistical victims/groups represented by numerical information. This may indicate conceptual ambiguity in the stimulus or interpretation and could affect whether participants compare one identified child to a group, a single unidentified person, or an abstract population.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim

issues.subcategory: Scale anchors and item wording omitted for donation and feelings
issues.description: The manuscript does not report exact response options, anchors, or whether donation was entered as integer dollars or continuous amount. It also omits item wording and scales for affective feelings, moral responsibility, appropriateness, and perceived impact. These are required to evaluate measurement validity and replicate the study.
issues.quote: donation and feeling variables as the dependent variables respectively

issues.subcategory: Correlation interpreted predictively from cross-sectional condition data
issues.description: The manuscript says correlations examine whether affective feelings predict donation. Correlation between simultaneously measured self-reports and donation intentions cannot establish prediction in a causal or temporal sense, particularly when feelings may be post-decision rationalizations. The wording should be associational unless temporal ordering and modeling justify prediction.
issues.quote: We conducted a correlation between aggregated feelings and donation to examine whether affective feelings predict donation.

issues.subcategory: Mediation/mechanism claims not tested
issues.description: The introduction emphasizes affective feelings and perceived impact as mechanisms, but the analyses only test mean differences and correlations. No mediation or causal mechanism model is preregistered or reported. Therefore claims about affective feelings accounting for donation differences or perceived impact being linked mechanistically are unsupported.
issues.quote: The second goal of the current research is to examine the effect of affective feelings on the studied phenomenon, with the introduction of an extension known as the perceived impact of donation.

issues.subcategory: Condition-specific correlations underpowered relative to total N and multiple comparisons
issues.description: Although total N is 1000, condition-specific correlations have n around 159-175. The manuscript tests six correlations without a clear correction plan or power analysis for correlations. Null correlations may reflect limited power for small effects, and multiple comparisons increase false positive risk.
issues.quote: correlation between aggregated feelings and donation across six different conditions

issues.subcategory: Table numbering inconsistent
issues.description: The manuscript references Table 7 as classification of replication before Table 6 appears, then later uses Table 7 for donation descriptives. This creates confusion and suggests insufficient editorial control over reporting.
issues.quote: Table 7 summarizes the current replication as a "close to very close replication".

issues.subcategory: External supplementary links used for essential details
issues.description: Essential methodological information—including power analysis, full design, procedure, materials, comparisons/deviations, and open-science disclosures—is deferred to external documents and folders. A manuscript should contain enough detail in the main text to evaluate and replicate the study, with supplements as support rather than replacement.
issues.quote: The session of “Procedure” in the supplementary summarizes the procedure of the current replication study.

issues.subcategory: No control for previous MTurk exposure or duplicate participation
issues.description: MTurk participants may have completed similar identifiable victim/donation studies before. The manuscript excludes self-reported prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect but does not mention preventing duplicate participation, screening prior related studies, or using worker IDs. Prior exposure could alter responses to both manipulation and outcome.
issues.quote: We will recruit participants on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform

issues.subcategory: Updated victim information may change severity and emotional content
issues.description: Changing the victim information from the original stimuli to current Save the Children content may alter vividness, need severity, credibility, familiarity, and emotional salience. These are core to the identifiable victim effect. The manuscript does not report equivalence testing or stimulus validation.
issues.quote: Updated victim information  We will present the participants with the most updated victim information retrieved from the website of Save the Children

issues.subcategory: No demographic covariates or sample characteristics beyond age/gender
issues.description: The manuscript reports only age and gender for the dummy sample and not education, income, political ideology, religiosity, parental status, prior donation behavior, or country—variables plausibly related to charitable giving. While covariates may not be necessary for randomized experiments, they are important for describing MTurk samples and diagnosing imbalance, especially if participants self-select conditions.
issues.quote: Gender | Not specified | 529 males, 471 females

issues.subcategory: Claim that original effects are medium questionable
issues.description: The manuscript states all Study 1 effects were medium, including d = -0.36 and d = 0.41. Under conventional benchmarks, these are small-to-medium, not clearly medium. Overstating original effect magnitude can affect expectations and interpretation of replication success.
issues.quote: The effect sizes were all considered as medium

issues.subcategory: Misuse of 'debiasing' without normative benchmark
issues.description: The study labels reductions in donation to identifiable victims as 'debiasing,' but it does not establish a normative standard for optimal donation or whether lower giving to identifiable victims is normatively better than higher giving to statistical victims. Without measuring efficiency, charity effectiveness, or moral criteria, 'debiasing' may be theoretically loaded.
issues.quote: examine the effect of deliberative thinking on debiasing the identifiable victim effect

issues.subcategory: Original Study 3 description conflicts with current factorial comparison
issues.description: Original Study 3 had three identifiability conditions and no explicit intervention, but the replication compares intervention and no-intervention across all three identifiability levels. Therefore the replication's Study 3-related hypotheses and comparisons are not directly comparable to the original Study 3 effect.
issues.quote: The third group was considered as a joint condition provided with both statistical and identifiable victim information.

issues.subcategory: No preregistered primary outcome identified
issues.description: The manuscript includes donation, aggregated feelings, segregated feelings, perceived impact, and correlations, but does not clearly identify the primary endpoint or hierarchy of hypotheses. Without a primary outcome, interpretation of mixed findings is vulnerable to selective emphasis.
issues.quote: donation and feeling variables as the dependent variables respectively

issues.subcategory: Use of Bonferroni post-hoc for interaction not appropriate as described
issues.description: The table suggests Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons for 'interaction of identifiability and intervention.' Pairwise comparisons of main-effect marginal means do not test interaction patterns. Interaction follow-up should involve simple effects or planned interaction contrasts aligned with hypotheses.
issues.quote: Bonferroni -adjusted pairwise comparisons ... c. interaction of identifiability and intervention on donation (with joint condition)

issues.subcategory: No software versions or analysis code details in manuscript
issues.description: The manuscript says JAMOVI and R were used but does not report versions, packages, functions, contrast coding, sums-of-squares type, or treatment of unequal cell sizes. These choices can affect ANOVA results in unbalanced factorial designs.
issues.quote: We conducted the data analysis with JAMOVI for statistical testing and R for calculation of 95%CI

issues.subcategory: Unbalanced design without ANOVA sums-of-squares specification
issues.description: Cell sizes differ across the 2 x 3 design. In unbalanced ANOVA, Type I, II, and III sums of squares can yield different tests, especially with interactions. The manuscript does not specify the sums-of-squares type or contrast coding used.

issues.subcategory: Potential demand characteristics from explicit teaching manipulation
issues.description: Explicitly teaching participants about the identifiable victim effect immediately before asking for a donation may produce demand characteristics or reactance rather than deliberative thought. The original study has the same concern, but the replication should address whether participants inferred the hypothesis, especially in an online setting.
issues.quote: participants under manipulation were taught about the identifiable victim effect before donating to the victims

issues.subcategory: Perceived impact measured post-treatment and potentially post-donation
issues.description: The original and replication procedures appear to collect feeling/evaluation variables after donation. If perceived impact is measured after the donation decision, it may be a consequence or rationalization of donation rather than a cause. Claims that perceived impact affects donation require temporal ordering or mediation design.
issues.quote: After the donation, they had to fill up a questionnaire for different cognitive evaluations they experienced which may influence their choice of donation.

issues.subcategory: Donation appropriateness included as affective reaction
issues.description: Donation appropriateness is an evaluative/normative judgment rather than an affective feeling. Treating it as part of an aggregated affective-feelings score may obscure the distinction between emotion, moral judgment, and perceived efficacy.
issues.quote: Segregated feelings include being upset, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, and donation appropriateness

issues.subcategory: Original article citation metadata inconsistently capitalized/misspelled
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly misspells 'Slovic' as 'Solvic' and inconsistently capitalizes journal titles. While not a validity issue by itself, it signals carelessness in reporting and may impair accurate citation tracking.
issues.quote: Solvic (2010)

issues.subcategory: p-value notation for original Study 1 incomplete
issues.description: Original Study 1 p-values are reported only as '<.05' despite exact F statistics and degrees of freedom being available. Exact p-values would improve comparability and allow accurate effect-size verification. This is a reporting limitation for replication evaluation.

issues.subcategory: No description of charity credibility or current context controls
issues.description: The original donation was to Save the Children in a specific context. The replication uses updated information but does not report whether participants were asked about charity familiarity, trust, prior donations, or skepticism about online donation prompts. Such variables can influence donation independently of victim identifiability.
issues.quote: the perceived trustworthiness of the charity, the expected accountability of funds, evaluation of organizational efficiency

issues.subcategory: Funding acquisition listed despite no financial support
issues.description: The declaration says no financial support was received, but the CRediT table lists funding acquisition for Gilad. This inconsistency should be clarified, although it is not central to scientific validity.
issues.quote: Financial Disclosure/Funding: The author(s) received no financial support

issues.subcategory: No participant-flow diagram
issues.description: For an online preregistered experiment with exclusions for prior knowledge and attention checks, a participant-flow report is needed: recruited, consented, randomized/assigned, excluded by reason, analyzed per condition. The manuscript lacks this information.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.subcategory: Residual df assumes no exclusions despite exclusion statement
issues.description: The ANOVA residual df is 994, implying exactly N=1000 for a 2 x 3 between-subjects ANOVA. Yet the manuscript says participants with prior knowledge and failed attention checks were excluded. If exclusions occurred, the generated initial N and analyzed N should differ. This inconsistency likely stems from dummy data but would be invalid in a final report.
issues.quote: Residual ... Replication | 994

issues.subcategory: No control for order if truly within-subject
issues.description: If the design is actually within-subject, the manuscript does not describe order randomization/counterbalancing, washout, or how exposure to multiple victim descriptions avoids carryover and contrast effects. These are critical because identifiability effects are sensitive to separate versus joint evaluation.
issues.quote: single within-subject design

issues.subcategory: Separate versus joint evaluation framework insufficiently handled
issues.description: The identifiable victim effect differs in separate versus joint evaluation; the manuscript merges conditions and introduces a joint condition while also using between-condition comparisons. It does not adequately distinguish whether observed effects reflect identifiability, joint evaluation, comparison mode, or deliberation.
issues.quote: jointly presenting an identifiable victim and statistical victims together would diminish sympathy towards the identifiable victim because the calculative mode of thinking is being activated while comparing two situations simultaneously.

issues.subcategory: No details on payment/endowment framing
issues.description: The original endowed participants with five one-dollar bills from a prior survey. The replication says no reward from a pre-survey and compensation is unspecified, but does not specify how the hypothetical $5 was framed. Endowment and earned-money framing are central to donation behavior.
issues.quote: No reward acquired from a pre-survey  Participants will not conduct an irrelevant survey prior to the experiment to earn $5 for the donation

issues.subcategory: Use of LeBel replication evaluation criteria compromised by non-comparable effect
issues.description: The manuscript proposes comparing the replication effect to the original d=.48, but the replication changes the outcome, sample, design, and conditions. The replication effect from a 2x3 hypothetical-donation design is not directly comparable to the original 2x2 real-donation effect without defining an equivalent contrast.
issues.quote: We aim to study the effect ... by comparing the replication effect with the original effect (d = 0.48, 95% CI [0.11, 0.84])
